testCases.name: test_case_0
testCases.input: why can't we test an LLM app the same way we test normal software?
testCases.actualOutput:
Because the whole idea of “testing” in software is built on the assumption that the system behaves the same way every time you give it the same input. In a traditional program, if you run a calculator with the input “2 + 2” you will always get “4.” If you give a login form the right credentials you always get a successful login, and if you give the wrong ones you always get a failure. That determinism lets you write a handful of test cases, run them, and say “this version passes all the tests, the next version fails one of them, so we know exactly what changed.”

Large‑language‑model (LLM) applications break that assumption. They are probabilistic: the same prompt can produce different answers on different runs, or even on the same run if the model’s internal state changes. Because of that, you can’t simply write a fixed set of inputs and expect a fixed set of outputs to compare against. You need to evaluate across many runs, many prompts, and many criteria—correctness, clarity, relevance to the course content, safety, etc.—to get a meaningful picture of performance. In short, the deterministic nature of conventional software lets you use straightforward test cases, whereas the probabilistic, context‑sensitive behavior of LLMs requires a more nuanced, repeatable, and criteria‑driven evaluation approach.
testCases.expectedOutput: Normal software is deterministic and rule-based, so the same input always gives the same output and you can assert one exact expected value. LLM applications are probabilistic, so the same input can produce different wordings, and most tasks have many acceptable answers instead of one exact string. That breaks exact-match testing, so LLM evaluation instead judges qualities of the output, usually against a golden dataset and often with an LLM as a judge.

testCases.name: test_case_1
testCases.input: what's the difference between model evals and application evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
Model evals and application evals are two ways we look at an LLM, but they focus on different things.  

When we talk about **model evals**, we’re looking straight at the LLM itself. Think of it as a lab test for the model: we give it a set of standard questions or tasks—like knowledge, reasoning, or math problems—and see how well it does. These are the benchmarks that show a new LLM “came on top” on a leaderboard. If you need to compare one model to another, you run these model evals. You can also create your own custom model evals if you want to see how a model behaves on a particular dataset that matters to you, but the goal is still to measure the model’s raw capabilities.

**Application evals**, on the other hand, are about the LLM in action. Here we evaluate an entire system that uses the LLM—say a chatbot, a recommendation engine, or a dashboard that relies on the model’s output. The focus shifts from the model’s isolated performance to how well the application works for its users. We might run the same LLM on a custom set of application‑specific prompts, or use a tool like the LMEvaluation harness to test fine‑tuned models in the context of the application. The idea is to see whether the LLM, when wrapped in the application, meets the real‑world needs of that use case.

So, in short: model evals test the LLM’s inherent abilities with generic or custom benchmarks, while application evals test how those abilities translate into a finished product that people actually use.
testCases.expectedOutput: Model evals test the capabilities of the raw LLM itself, independent of any product, and include benchmarks as well as custom model evals used to pick a model. Application evals test a system built around one or more LLMs, such as a RAG chatbot or an agent, evaluated end-to-end. In short, model evals judge the model, application evals judge the system you built.

testCases.name: test_case_2
testCases.input: what are the different methods to actually perform an eval?
testCases.actualOutput:
In the course we’ve covered three distinct ways to run an evaluation, each suited to a different kind of task or resource.

First, **programmatic methods** let you write code that automatically checks the model’s output against a reference or a set of rules. For example, in the Zomato email‑categorization app we used a Python script to compute accuracy by comparing the LLM’s labels to the ground‑truth labels in our dataset. This approach is fast, repeatable, and works well when you have a clear metric you can compute in code.

Second, you can use the **LLM itself as a judge**. Here the model evaluates its own or another model’s responses, often by scoring or ranking them. In the UPSC mock‑test example we built a golden dataset and had the LLM act as a judge, scoring how well it could evaluate the test answers. This method is handy when you want the model to apply domain‑specific knowledge or nuanced judgment that is hard to encode in a simple script.

Third, there’s **human evaluation**. Human raters read the model’s outputs and provide qualitative or quantitative feedback. This is the gold standard when you need nuanced judgments, such as measuring safety or user satisfaction, that are difficult for automated metrics to capture.

So, the three methods we’ve discussed are programmatic evaluation, LLM‑based judging, and human evaluation. Each has its own strengths and is often used in combination to get a comprehensive view of a model’s performance.
testCases.expectedOutput: There are three broad methods. Programmatic (deterministic) evaluation uses code and fixed rules to check the output, which is cheap and reliable but only works when correctness can be expressed in code. LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable LLM to score outputs, which handles subjective or semantic judgments at scale. Human evaluation uses people to judge outputs, which is the most reliable for nuanced quality but the slowest and most expensive.

testCases.name: test_case_3
testCases.input: what does reference-based vs reference-free eval mean?
testCases.actualOutput:
In the context of evaluating language‑model chatbots, “reference‑based” and “reference‑free” simply describe whether you have a pre‑written, correct answer to compare against.

A **reference‑based evaluation** is one where you already have a golden dataset—a set of questions paired with the correct answers. You run the chatbot on those questions and then measure how close its responses are to the reference answers. Think of it like grading a test where the teacher has the answer key. The UPSC exam example from the lecture is a classic case of this: the model’s output is judged against a known correct answer.

A **reference‑free evaluation**, on the other hand, is used when you don’t have a predetermined answer key. Instead, you assess the model’s output using other criteria, such as whether it hallucinated facts or how well it follows instructions. In the lecture, the example of measuring hallucination rate—checking if the chatbot is making up information—illustrates a reference‑free approach. Here, you’re not comparing to a gold answer; you’re judging the response based on other standards.

So, the key difference is: reference‑based relies on a known correct answer to compare against, while reference‑free evaluates the output without any pre‑written answer key.
testCases.expectedOutput: A reference-based eval needs a ground-truth answer to compare against, a golden or expected output authored ahead of time, and scores the system by how close it comes to that reference. A reference-free eval needs no ground truth and instead judges an intrinsic property of the output, usually with an LLM as a judge. The test is simply whether the metric requires an expected answer.

testCases.name: test_case_4
testCases.input: offline eval vs online eval - what's the difference?
testCases.actualOutput:
Offline evaluation and online evaluation are two sides of the same coin when it comes to checking how a language‑model‑based system behaves, but they serve different purposes and run in different environments.

**Offline evaluation** happens before you ship anything to users. You build a fixed, curated set of test cases—often called a “golden” data set—where you already know what the correct answer should be. You run your model on that data, compare its outputs to the gold answers, and compute metrics like accuracy, precision, or safety scores. Because the data set is small and the evaluation is deterministic, this process is fast, cheap, and repeatable. It’s the tool you use for *gating*: if the score you get is above a pre‑set threshold, you can confidently push the new code into production via continuous integration. In short, offline eval tells you whether the application is **working correctly** according to a known standard.

**Online evaluation** takes place after the system is live and interacting with real users. Here you don’t have a pre‑defined answer key; instead, you monitor the system’s behavior on the actual traffic it receives. Since a production bot might talk to tens of thousands of people a day, evaluating every single conversation would be prohibitively expensive. That’s why a sampling technique is used: you randomly pick a subset of conversations—say 1,000 out of 50,000—to keep costs down while still getting a representative picture. Online eval’s main job is *drift detection*: it tells you whether the system is still running normally in the real world, catching emergent bugs or performance regressions that offline tests might miss. Because it operates on live data, it’s more costly and slower, but it’s essential for ensuring that the deployed software continues to behave as expected.

So, the key differences are:

- **When they run**: offline before deployment, online after deployment.
- **Data**: offline uses a fixed, golden data set; online uses live production traffic, sampled to reduce cost.
- **Answer key**: offline has a known correct answer; online does not.
- **Purpose**: offline checks correctness against a standard; online checks ongoing health and drift in production.
- **Cost and speed**: offline is cheap and fast; online is more expensive and slower but necessary for real‑world monitoring.

Both types of evaluation are complementary. You need offline eval to gate new releases and online eval to keep the system healthy once it’s in the hands of users.
testCases.expectedOutput: Offline eval happens before deployment on a fixed golden dataset in a controlled setting; it is usually reference-based and is what you run during development to decide whether a version is good enough to ship. Online eval happens after deployment on live production traffic, works without ground-truth labels, and relies on real user interactions and signals like thumbs up/down, latency, and cost. Offline gates deployment; online monitors real behaviour.

testCases.name: test_case_5
testCases.input: what is drift and why does it matter after deployment?
testCases.actualOutput:
Drift, in the context of LLM‑based systems, is the gradual change that happens to the data and the environment after a model has been deployed. Think of it as the difference between the world the model was trained on and the world it actually sees once it’s live. Over time, the documents, pricing tables, curriculum pages, policies, and even user queries that the system encounters can shift. For example, a course price might be updated, a curriculum might be revised, or new types of emails might start arriving. These changes mean that the assumptions the model made during offline evaluation no longer hold true.

Why does this matter after deployment? Because the offline evaluation you performed before launch was based on a snapshot of the system’s content and usage patterns. Once the system is in production, that snapshot becomes stale. If you don’t account for drift, the model’s performance can degrade: it might give less faithful answers, misclassify new kinds of emails, or become slower under increased load. In practice, you monitor metrics like faithfulness over time; a sudden drop in the last few hours signals drift. When drift is detected, you alert, investigate, and then feed the new, problematic examples back into your golden dataset. This enriches the offline evaluation set so that future retraining or fine‑tuning reflects the current reality.

In short, drift is the mismatch that grows between the model’s training world and the live world. It matters after deployment because it can render your previously accurate, offline‑tested system unreliable, and it forces you to keep monitoring, updating, and improving both the model and the evaluation data to maintain quality.
testCases.expectedOutput: Drift is the gradual degradation of a deployed system's performance over time as real-world data or usage patterns move away from what the system was built and evaluated on. Users may start asking new kinds of questions or the knowledge base may go stale, so metrics slowly fall even though the code did not change. It matters because these failures appear silently in production, so you monitor metrics over time, set alerts when they drop, and feed failing cases back into your offline dataset.

testCases.name: test_case_6
testCases.input: why do we need multiple eval pipelines for a single application instead of just one?
testCases.actualOutput:
In an LLM‑based application you rarely have just one place where things can go wrong, and you rarely care about only one kind of risk. That’s why we almost always set up several evaluation pipelines instead of a single one.

First, think about the different layers of the system. A typical application has a **retrieval** component, a **generation** component, and then the overall **workflow** that stitches them together. Each of these layers can fail in its own way—retrieval might pull the wrong documents, the generator might hallucinate, or the workflow might mis‑order steps. If you only had one eval pipeline, you would have to try to catch all those failures in one place, which would make the pipeline very complex and hard to interpret. By giving each layer its own pipeline you can isolate the source of a problem: is it the retriever, the generator, or the orchestration?

Second, the kinds of risks you want to monitor are not all the same. In the RAG chatbot example we talked about three distinct pipelines: one for **latency** (how fast the system responds), one for **safety** (does it produce harmful content), and one for **correctness** (does it give the right answer). Each of these metrics has its own measurement methods and thresholds. Mixing them into a single pipeline would blur the signals and make it hard to decide whether a failure is a latency issue, a safety issue, or a correctness issue.

So, in short, we need multiple eval pipelines because an LLM application has multiple failure points—component, workflow, and application level—and because we want to monitor multiple risk categories that each require its own metrics and thresholds. This separation makes the evaluation clearer, more actionable, and easier to maintain.
testCases.expectedOutput: Because a single LLM application has multiple failure points and multiple risk categories, so one eval cannot cover it. There are different failure points at the component, workflow, and application levels, and each needs its own eval. There are also different risk categories, quality, safety, and operations, that require different metrics. So you build several eval pipelines and run them together as an eval suite.

testCases.name: test_case_7
testCases.input: what are the different risk categories we evaluate an LLM app on?
testCases.actualOutput:
When we talk about evaluating an LLM‑based application, we usually break the risks into three broad buckets that the course calls out.

First, **application quality**. This is the set of risks that tell us whether the model is actually doing what the user asked. It covers things like correctness and accuracy—does the answer reflect what the model really knows? Relevance—does it stay on topic? Completeness—does it answer every part of the user’s question? And instruction‑following—if we ask it to produce a specific format or length, does it comply? These are the core quality checks that let us know the app is delivering useful, trustworthy content.

Second, **safety**. Safety risks are about what the model should *not* do. In the context of Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) or any LLM app, we worry about leaking private context, being tricked into jailbreak or other malicious behavior, or otherwise producing disallowed content. All of these fall under the safety umbrella.

Third, **operations**. This category looks at the practical side of deployment: can the app run fast enough, can it be run cheaply, and does it remain reliable over time? Operational risks are about performance, cost, and stability rather than the content itself.

So, in short, the three risk categories we evaluate an LLM app on are application quality, safety, and operations.
testCases.expectedOutput: There are three risk categories. Quality checks whether the output is good, for example correct, relevant, and grounded. Safety checks whether the output is harmful, for example toxic content, leaking personal information, or being jailbroken. Operations checks the running characteristics of the system such as latency, cost, and token usage. A full eval suite covers all three, not just quality.

testCases.name: test_case_8
testCases.input: as an AI engineer why do I even need model evals?
testCases.actualOutput:
As an AI engineer, you’re constantly juggling choices about which language model to put in the “brain” of your application. Model evaluations give you the yardstick you need to make those choices confidently. First, they let you compare two or more models side‑by‑side—so if you’re deciding between Claude’s Opus 4.8 and the newer Fable, you can look at concrete numbers rather than guesswork. That comparison is essential when a manager asks whether a newer model actually delivers better performance for your specific use case.

Second, model evals let you track progress over time. When a new version of a model lands, you can run the same benchmark and see whether it truly improves on the last one. Without those metrics, you’d be blind to whether a new release is worth the effort of redeploying or re‑training your system.

Third, they help you understand where your own application might be falling short. If your RAG pipeline isn’t meeting expectations, you can isolate whether the issue lies in the retriever, the generator, or the underlying embedding model. Model evals give you a clear signal about which component needs tweaking.

Finally, they’re the only systematic way to justify decisions to stakeholders. When you present a scorecard that shows a new model’s strengths and weaknesses, you can back up your recommendation with data instead of intuition. In short, model evaluations are the compass that keeps your engineering decisions on track, lets you measure improvement, and provides the evidence you need to deploy the best possible LLM for your application.
testCases.expectedOutput: Because you have to choose which model to use for your application, and model evals give you a concrete, measurable basis for that decision rather than guessing. Benchmarks let you compare general capabilities of models, and when you need to know which model is best for your specific task you run custom model evals on your own data. Without model evals you cannot justify model selection objectively.

testCases.name: test_case_9
testCases.input: what is a benchmark and what does MMLU test?
testCases.actualOutput:
A benchmark is a standardized, shared test that every model can run on the same set of questions. Because the questions and scoring are identical for all models, you can directly compare their numbers and see which one performs better on that particular task. Think of it like a common exam that every student takes; the scores tell you how each student did relative to the others.

MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is one of those benchmarks. It was created to probe a model’s breadth of knowledge across many subjects—everything from science and history to literature and math. The test presents a wide range of multiple‑choice questions that cover a broad curriculum, so a model that truly “understands” many domains will do well. In practice, MMLU has also highlighted that models that are good at reasoning can get an extra edge, because some of the questions are designed to benefit from logical deduction. So, in short, MMLU is a benchmark that measures how much general knowledge and reasoning a language model has across a diverse set of topics.

MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) is a multiple-choice benchmark covering many subjects that measures the breadth of a model's knowledge. It does not measure reasoning depth, calibration, open-ended generation, and it is English and exam-style only.
